question: How does Deb Liu explain treating product growth as a “game of inches,” and why does she favor shipping many small experiments over waiting for a perfect plan?
evidence_quote: if you can move things 1% a little bit faster every single week, think about the amount of growth you get at the end.
expected_points: Small improvements can compound into substantial growth over time.
Shipping many experiments helps teams learn what works and what doesn’t.
Improving the experiments’ success rate creates more wins without requiring a perfect plan.

answer.summary: Deb Liu says growth usually comes from small gains that accumulate, not one magic-bullet leap. She favors shipping many hypotheses because failed experiments teach the team what to change, while successful ones add up to meaningful output.

sections.heading: Growth as a game of inches
sections.content: Rather than focus only on a dramatic step change, Liu looks for small improvements that compound: moving a metric 1% a little faster each week, or growing by single-digit increments. Small, seemingly simple changes can matter—for example, adding a “create an ad” link next to ads helped people find the ad-creation flow. On a payments growth team, she recalls working from a list of 100 hypotheses and tackling them in batches of 10 through sprint cycles.

sections.heading: Why ship many experiments
sections.content: Liu argues against overthinking until there is a perfect plan: it is okay if 80% of ideas do not work, because those failures provide learning. Her comparison is that shipping 20 things with a 20% success rate yields four successes—the same number as shipping four things if all four succeed—while also revealing what did not work. If the success rate rises from 20% to 30%, 20 attempts yield six successes, or 50% more than four. She describes growth as a learning engine: use results to reiterate, change course, and improve.

answer.summary: Liu says growth usually comes from small gains that accumulate, not one magic-bullet leap. Shipping more experiments lets teams learn what works and what does not sooner than waiting for a perfect plan. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: Growth as a game of inches
sections.content: Rather than focus only on a huge step change, Liu recommends looking for small opportunities and stacking them: even moving something 1% faster each week can add up, and growth can come in single-digit increments. She gives Facebook’s “create an ad” link as an example: a small addition helped people find the ads flow and became a major growth driver. [S1]

sections.heading: Why ship many experiments
sections.content: Liu says teams can overthink growth by waiting for a perfect battle plan. On a payments-growth team, they kept a list of 100 hypotheses, worked through the first 10 and then the next 10 in sprint cycles, and used the same approach on ads and marketplace. She says it is fine if 80% of ideas fail. For comparison, a team shipping 20 things with a 20% success rate gets four wins—the same number as shipping four things—and also learns what failed. At a 30% success rate, 20 experiments yield six wins, which she describes as 50% more output, alongside those lessons. She frames growth as a learning machine: iterate on what works, change what does not, and keep improving. [S2]
